title: Rates and Equilibrium
seo_title: Year 11 Science: Rates and Equilibrium Worksheets (GCSE Combined Science)
standard_code: KS4 Chemistry: The rate and extent of chemical change
standard_text: Calculating rates of reactions; factors which affect the rates of chemical reactions (concentration, pressure, surface area, temperature, catalysts); collision theory and activation energy; reversible reactions and energy changes; equilibrium; (higher tier) the effect of changing conditions on equilibrium (Le Chatelier's principle).
meta_desc: Free Year 11 GCSE Combined Science worksheets on rates of reaction and equilibrium: mean rate, collision theory, temperature and concentration, catalysts, reversible reactions and Le Chatelier's principle. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Mean rate = amount of product ÷ time.
key_sub: More frequent, more energetic collisions mean a faster rate.
body_html:
How to think about it

Reactions speed up when particles collide more often or with more energy.

  • Mean rate = volume of gas (cm³) ÷ time (s), or mass lost (g) ÷ time (s).
  • Concentration, pressure, surface area and temperature increase the rate. A catalyst lowers the activation energy.
  • In a closed system a reversible reaction reaches equilibrium: forward and reverse rates are equal.
Example

60 cm³ of gas in 30 s. Mean rate?

60 ÷ 30

Answer: 2 cm³/s

Example

Forward reaction endothermic. Reverse?

Opposite direction

Answer: exothermic

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a catalyst is used up.
  • Thinking a longer time means a faster reaction.
  • Thinking the reactions stop at equilibrium.

faq.q: How do you calculate a mean rate of reaction?
faq.a: Divide the amount of product made (or reactant used) by the time taken, for example cm³ of gas ÷ seconds.

faq.q: How does temperature affect the rate?
faq.a: At a higher temperature particles move faster, so they collide more often and more collisions have at least the activation energy.
The forward and reverse reactions continue at the same rate, so the amounts of reactants and products stay constant.

items.q: Does a catalyst change the position of equilibrium?
c: No. It makes equilibrium reached faster.
items.e: Both directions speed up equally.

items.q: An engineer wants more SO<sub>3</sub> from making sulfuric acid (contact process): 2SO<sub>2</sub> + O<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2SO<sub>3</sub>, the energy change = −198 kJ. Which single change increases the amount of SO<sub>3</sub> at equilibrium?
c: The pressure is decreased (the container is made larger).
items.e: the energy change = −198 kJ, so the forward reaction is exothermic. Cooling favors the exothermic direction.

items.q: In making ammonia (Haber process): N<sub>2</sub> + 3H<sub>2</sub> ⇌ 2NH<sub>3</sub>, the energy change = −92 kJ. Some N<sub>2</sub> is removed. How does the equilibrium respond?

items.e: Both sides have 2 mol of gas, so pressure has no effect.

items.q: What does Le Chatelier's principle say?
c: If a condition changes, the equilibrium shifts to counteract the change.
items.e: Higher tier.
